content: The linking number is a mathematical invariant that quantifies the linking of two closed curves in three-dimensional space. It represents the number of times one curve winds around the other. The linking number is always an integer, which can be positive or negative depending on the orientation of the curves. This concept was introduced by Carl Friedrich Gauss through the linking integral. It is a fundamental object of study in knot theory, algebraic topology, and differential geometry, with applications in various scientific fields, including quantum mechanics, electromagnetism, and the study of DNA supercoiling. Definition For any two closed curves in space, they can be manipulated into a standard position without intersecting each other. This process determines the linking number. While each curve may pass through itself during this motion, the two curves must remain distinct and separate throughout. Computing the Linking Number The linking number of two curves can be computed using an algorithm based on a link diagram. Each crossing in the diagram is labeled as positive or negative according to specific rules. The linking number is then calculated as half the difference between the total number of positive crossings and the total number of negative crossings. Alternatively, the linking number can be expressed using sums of specific types of crossings, where the difference between certain crossing counts corresponds to the linking number. Properties and Examples Two unlinked curves always have a linking number of zero. Reversing the orientation of one curve negates the linking number, while reversing the orientation of both curves leaves it unchanged. The linking number is chiral, meaning that taking the mirror image of a link negates the linking number. The convention for positive linking numbers is based on the right-hand rule. The winding number of an oriented curve in the x-y plane is equal to its linking number with the z-axis, which is treated as a closed curve in the 3-sphere. If one of the curves is simple, the first homology group of its complement is isomorphic to the integers (Z). In this case, the linking number is determined by the homology class of the other curve. In physics, the linking number is an example of a topological quantum number and is related to quantum entanglement. Gauss's Integral Definition For two non-intersecting differentiable curves, (gamma_1) and (gamma_2), the Gauss map is defined from the torus to the sphere. A point on the unit sphere corresponds to a crossing in the link diagram, where (gamma_1) passes over (gamma_2). The orientation of the neighborhood around this point determines the sign of the crossing. To compute the linking number, one counts the signed number of times the Gauss map covers a point on the sphere. This is equivalent to the degree of the Gauss map, which is invariant under isotopy. The linking number can also be expressed as a double line integral, known as the Gauss linking integral: [ oint_{gamma_1} oint_{gamma_2} frac{mathbf{r}_1 mathbf{r}_2}{|mathbf{r}_1 mathbf{r}_2|^3} cdot (dmathbf{r}_1 times dmathbf{r}_2). ] This integral computes the total signed area of the image of the Gauss map, normalized by the area of the sphere (4π). Generalizations Just as closed curves can be linked in three dimensions, any two closed manifolds of dimensions (m) and (n) can be linked in a Euclidean space of dimension (m + n + 1). The associated Gauss map's degree generalizes the concept of the linking number. A framed knot has a self-linking number, which is computed by considering the linking number of the knot with a slightly displaced version of itself along the framing vectors. The self-linking number obtained by vertical displacement (blackboard framing) is known as Kauffman's self-linking number. Notes The labeling of crossings used to compute the linking number is the same as that used for the writhe of a knot, but only crossings involving both curves of the link are considered. The Jordan curve theorem implies that if one curve is simple, the linking number can be interpreted as the number of times the other curve crosses in and out of the region bounded by the simple curve.
